title: CuriousTogether: Implications of Curiosity and Cultural Grounding in Multi-Agent LLM Interactions
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings, exhibiting emergent collective behaviors, yet the role of curiosity as a driver of such dynamics remains understudied. We introduce CuriousTogether, a framework evaluating curiosity-driven multi-agent LLM interactions across three complementary dimensions: novelty-seeking, epistemic and social curiosity. Across eight tasks spanning reasoning, creative generation, and social bias mitigation, curiosity-guided multi-agent settings yield improvements over non-curious ones on seven out of eight tasks, with gains of up to 20.6% in story generation (semantic diversity) and a 14.9 pp reduction in stereotype rates. Furthermore, country-conditioned cultural grounding show benefits for story generation and social tasks, but can hurt precision-oriented reasoning. Finally, we show that inference-time multi-agent curiosity-based approach offers favorable quality-token trade-offs, compared with single-agent baselines. Together, these findings support curiosity-guided interaction as a practical mechanism for improving multi-agent collaboration, with downstream benefits for reasoning, creative, and societal tasks.

title: Multi-Estimate Elicitation Does Not Uniformly Debias Language Model Judgments
summary: Does eliciting five weighted estimates within a single response consistently improve numerical judgments? We compare direct and multi-estimate elicitation across anchoring, hindsight, base-rate, conjunction, and status-quo/default tasks in six frozen configurations. Each configuration contributes 618 admitted development units and 3,702 admitted formal units; the six-configuration formal cohort contains 22,212 units, including 21 missing outcomes. Of 45 preregistered confirmatory tests across five configurations, 12 reject on complete cases and 11 retain directional confirmation after the prespecified missingness-protection rule. Only one adjusted bound exceeds its smallest effect size of interest: gpt-oss-120b shows a 10.68-percentage-point increase in post-outcome confirmation error under multi-estimate elicitation (worst-case estimate 10.04 points). The remaining ten retained effects have sub-threshold point estimates; non-rejection does not establish equivalence. Joint presentation lowers signed conjunction excess in four confirmatory configurations, but this comparison changes both constraint visibility and call structure. Flash-high combines two disjoint execution-window batches under an approved continuation protocol, preserving their identities and non-causal interpretation. Post-hoc candidate-spread associations across all six configurations remain in-sample and require independent predictive validation. The completed cohort provides no evidence for uniform debiasing by multi-estimate elicitation. Materials: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies

title: Vision-Language Models Are Joint Denoisers in Robotic Action Generation
summary: Diffusion-based vision-language-action (VLA) models cascade pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with diffusion action experts, but typically restrict the VLM to providing static conditioning. This separation limits how much pretrained perception and reasoning can guide action generation, especially in out-of-distribution settings. We introduce JADE, a Joint Action DEnoiser that enables the VLM and action expert to jointly refine actions. Our key insight is that structured action latents allow the VLM to read the current noisy action together with visual observations and language instructions. At every denoising step, the VLM contextualizes the noisy action and guides the action expert through gated cross-attention, so that its guidance evolves with the action being generated. We further supervise the VLM to recover clean action latents from noisy ones, which gives it a direct action-learning signal and couples perception with control. Additionally, joint denoising enables JADE to generate actions with fewer sampling steps, helping offset the additional cost of VLM participation. An adaptive step-size schedule further balances task performance and inference latency. On RoboDojo, JADE achieves an average success rate of 12.67%, the highest among the evaluated $π_{0.5}$-based methods, and is competitive with recent VLA and WAM foundation models pretrained at scale. It also improves performance on RoboTwin 2.0 and raises the average success rate across four real-world bimanual tasks by 20.8 percentage points compared with $π_{0.5}$.

title: Learning to Group and Order: Cross-Instance Self-Supervised RL for Vision-Centric MLLMs
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become an important paradigm for improving multimodal large language models (MLLMs), especially with automatically verifiable rewards. Self-supervised visual pretext tasks provide such rewards without human annotations. However, existing methods mainly exploit within-instance structure, offering limited supervision for cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison. We introduce Group-and-Order Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning (GO-SSL), a cross-instance jigsaw framework for vision-centric MLLM post-training. Given two visual instances, GO-SSL mixes their local elements and trains the model to group them by instance of origin while recovering the order within each group, coupling instance-level comparison with spatial, temporal, or geometric structure recovery. This paired formulation turns the same unlabeled data into richer verifiable supervision through diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum. We instantiate GO-SSL mainly on cross-image jigsaw tasks and further extend it to 3D depth and video temporal ordering. Across diverse benchmarks, GO-SSL consistently improves over the base MLLM and prior self-supervised post-training baselines, with clear gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding. Further evaluations across model scales and families support its generality. These results suggest that cross-instance comparison provides a useful self-supervised RL signal for improving transferable visual understanding in MLLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/SEU-VIPGroup/GO-SSL.

title: VCoT-SQL: Enhancing Text-to-SQL Generation through Dual Chain-of-Thought Validation Training
summary: Open-source LLMs provide a flexible alternative to closed-source models for Text-to-SQL but still struggle with complex queries. Finetuning with chain-of-thought (CoT) data improves reasoning, yet standard datasets lack CoT annotations, requiring synthetic generation. Existing synthesis methods only verify the final answer, allowing flawed reasoning steps to corrupt the training data. We propose VCoT-SQL, a framework that improves Text-to-SQL generation through intermediate-step validated CoT supervision and a dedicated SQL validator, which enables small open-source models to outperform frontier closed-source models. VCoT-SQL trains two complementary models on curated reasoning traces: an SQL generator using clause-level CoT templates where reasoning steps are verified via execution and schema alignment checks, and an SQL validator using diagnostic CoT templates to detect syntactic, semantic, and type level errors. We further design a hierarchical schema filtering pipeline that integrates and refines complementary retrieval strategies to distill relevant database elements. VCoT-SQL achieves 66.82% execution accuracy on challenging dataset BIRD dev and 86.8% on Spider test, improving the base 7B model by 7% on BIRD. Notably, our CoT synthesis relies on 7B models yet outperforms methods that use 72B-scale or even proprietary closed source teachers for data generation, demonstrating that rigorous step-level validation can be more effective than scaling up teacher model size. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/INTREBID/VCoT-SQL.

title: Labadain-MedQA: A Tetun Medical QA Dataset for Fine-Tuning and Evaluating Large Language Models
summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have created opportunities for cross-lingual transfer of medical knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages to support access to healthcare information. However, medical question-answering (QA) datasets for fine-tuning and evaluating LLMs remain scarce for Tetun. To address this gap, we translated MedAlpaca's Medical Flashcards and WikiDoc Patient Information collections into Tetun using Gemini 2.5 Flash, producing 39,077 medical QA pairs. Translation quality was assessed on 50 randomly sampled QA pairs (100 documents) using automatic metrics against human reference translations and evaluations by two native Tetun-speaking healthcare professionals, focusing on medical accuracy and Tetun fluency. Human translations achieved higher mean ratings than LLM-generated translations for both criteria (4.43/5 vs. 4.02/5), with statistically significant differences (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.001). To assess downstream utility, we fine-tuned Gemma and Llama variants on the translated MedAlpaca dataset using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and evaluated them on 325 Tetun-translated United States Medical Licensing Examination multiple-choice questions. Gemma 4 12B fine-tuned using QLoRA achieved relative improvements in mean accuracy of 10.79% with 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) inference and 10.42% after merging the LoRA adapters into the BF16 base model, compared with the corresponding base models. These results highlight the viability of automatic dataset translation for Tetun medical QA and the effectiveness of PEFT in enhancing model performance. The datasets, models, and evaluation resources are accessible at https://github.com/labadain/labadain-medqa to support reproducible research on Tetun medical QA and facilitate machine translation, cross lingual, and multilingual research.

title: DramaVQA: Probing Detailed Understanding of Ultra-Long TV Dramas
summary: Despite recent progress in long-form video understanding, current benchmarks mostly focus on short clips or hour-scale videos. This leaves a major gap in evaluating ultra-long video understanding, where videos often last tens of hours. To bridge this gap, we introduce DramaVQA, a large-scale benchmark built upon long-form TV dramas. Containing approximately 20K question-answering (QA) pairs, the scale of DramaVQA exceeds previous long-video datasets, such as Video-MME and LVBench, by an order of magnitude. Our benchmark has two main features that make it stand out from existing datasets. First, we establish a scalable, LLM-assisted annotation pipeline that uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to generate complex questions, followed by strict human checking to ensure high data quality. Second, DramaVQA introduces a multi-level time structure; queries are designed across different video lengths, with the hardest questions requiring overall understanding across the entire drama. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art MLLMs face major challenges when tested on these very long videos, highlighting the need for agentic AI algorithms capable of managing long-term memory. The project is available at https://github.com/xinyuehuo/DramaVQA

title: How Close to the Theme? Similarity-Label Conditioning for Game Music Generation
summary: Composers develop music from an original idea, controlling how similar each new section is to it, from near repetition to new material. Game music needs this often, as its material repeats over long play. Music models, however, rarely learn to control similarity from real pieces. We further train a pretrained MIDI model on section pairs from Super Mario pieces. A label states each pair's similarity, and a context vector summarises the given section, or context. For 157 test contexts, the model generates six outputs per label. Twelve measures score the outputs; one main measure each covers melody, pitch content, rhythm and note length. On average, outputs requested as similar are more similar to their context than those requested as dissimilar, and not to other pieces. All twelve measures favour them; each main measure stays significant after correction for multiple tests. On melody, the gap comes mainly from more frequent restatement of the context's melody. Against an otherwise identical model without a label, only the request for high similarity makes outputs more similar. In a listening test, ratings followed melodic overlap with the context most closely of all measures.

title: ISBC: Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding of Pretrained Text Embeddings
summary: Pretrained text embeddings encode semantic structure in high-dimensional continuous spaces whose coordinates are difficult to interpret. We introduce Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding (ISBC), which learns a small set of binary dimensions from frozen embeddings without taxonomy labels or downstream outcomes. A trainable encoder and affine decoder combine reconstruction with controls on activity, factor utilization, dependence, and activation uncertainty. Individual bits and their conjunctions select overlapping document groups; complete activation profiles provide finer contexts for conditional comparisons. We evaluate these representations across corpora, backbones, and code configurations through reconstruction, geometry, predictive probes, and document inspection. Empirical cases identify both distinctions within existing categories and shared content across their boundaries. In a mixed-domain corpus, the most frequent profiles predominantly identify source collections, while selected within-source comparisons reveal sentiment and migration contrasts. Selected associations persist in additional documents encoded without refitting. In an engagement application, bits alone improve prediction of log-transformed outcomes over a constant reference, while their combinations identify within-event content contrasts associated with engagement. The results support using binary coordinates and their combinations for empirical interpretation, with complete profiles providing a fine, partly initialization-dependent description rather than a unique discrete taxonomy.

title: Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but which descriptions of people improve prediction when experimental designs change remains unclear. We develop a framework that draws candidate behavioral features from the literature and constructs profiles from earlier human experiments. An LLM-based profile generator assigns feature values from observed actions, messages, and surveys; a separate LLM simulates behavior using these profiles. By comparing simulated and observed outcomes in the training data, we select profile contents through forward feature selection, adding features while they improve prediction. We then evaluate the selected contents without modification against outcomes from new participants under new designs. Across 616 public-goods games, 144 multi-party bargaining games, and 1,480 generalized 11--20 money-request designs, leading one-feature profiles predict human outcome distributions better than no profile or general-purpose personas. Profiles with more features provide no clear additional benefit, and features' relative predictive value largely persists across learning and validation. Using profiles from one game family to simulate another produces uneven gains and can make predictions less accurate than simulations without profiles. The framework makes the choice of behavioral information a testable part of simulation design, helping researchers assess which descriptions remain useful as experimental conditions change.

title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization
summary: Using large language models to interpret experimental evidence, design discriminating experiments and formulate well-supported mechanistic explanations remains a central challenge in materials research. Here we establish PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark developed by perovskite researchers to evaluate scientific reasoning in perovskite photovoltaics. We also introduce OpenPerov, an expert-informed language-model framework that learns from expert-calibrated evidence records reconstructed from 4,035 training articles; these records link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic interpretations. Structured-evidence adaptation outperformed conventional question-answer training, and OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems. OpenPerov Pro raised Scientific Mastery further, from 87.6 to 89.1, by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. On questions derived from subsequent studies, both models also outscored expert-authored answers. In an experimental test of self-assembled monolayer design, OpenPerov selected a K analogue that outperformed the Na analogue preferred by experts. Devices incorporating the selected contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05% and retained 96.74% of their initial efficiency after 1,000 h of dark thermal ageing at 85 $^\circ$C. These results show that reconstructed scientific reasoning provides an effective basis for building domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design.

title: Answer Correction with Verifiable Rewards: A Gemma-Family Study of Multi-View Driving QA
summary: Multi-camera driving question answering provides a discrete test of vision-language models, but post-training gains can reflect changed selected answers or improved answer extraction. We investigate this distinction within the Gemma model family using archived, task-linked WaymoQA evaluations. A zero-shot diagnostic on 5,519 test questions spans effective-small, mixture-of-experts, unified, and dense checkpoints, with serving differences disclosed rather than interpreted as architecture effects. The strongest controlled evidence is a matched-harness Gemma-4-12B base/GRPO pair: accuracy rises from 73.78% to 75.43%, a gain of 1.65 percentage points with a scene-cluster bootstrap interval of [+0.84, +2.41]. There are 215 improvements and 124 regressions; 213 improvements start from an extractable but incorrect base answer, and only two recover previously unextractable responses. Crossing correctness with extraction state shows why correct noncompliant outputs cannot be counted as prediction errors. Category counts reveal a critical safety asymmetry: routine perception gains (+5.93 pp) mask a regression in safety-critical hazard prediction (-1.82 pp), demonstrating that unweighted outcome rewards can trade off rare edge cases for aggregate accuracy. Reward saturation describes sampled training dynamics rather than an architectural ceiling. A separate archived Gemma-31B thinking comparison yields no detected average improvement, with uncertainty that does not establish equivalence. These results support a modest answer-selection gain for the recorded tuning configuration and a reproducible diagnostic accounting, without attributing corrected labels to specific grounding mechanisms or claiming superiority over matched supervised tuning.

title: ProofPatch: Reviewing Lean Statements and Keeping the Reviews Valid as Formalizations Evolve
summary: The kernel of the Lean proof assistant checks that a proof establishes its statement. Whether the statement says what was intended is left to human reviewers. This is the old problem of validating a specification, and it grows more pressing as language models write formal statements in bulk and agents edit formal developments continuously. We present ProofPatch, a tool that helps reviewers judge Lean statements and keeps their judgments valid while the development changes. A reviewer can ask the kernel targeted questions about a statement, such as whether a hypothesis is needed or whether a counterexample exists. Each decision is stored with fingerprints of the statement as Lean elaborated it and of the definitions it depends on, and any declaration can be pinned so that a patch changing it is blocked, whether a person or an agent built on a large language model (LLM) wrote the patch. Working on elaborated terms rather than source text is the central design choice: notation and formatting changes leave a decision intact, and a changed definition reaches every theorem that uses it. On 229 pairs of consecutive revisions of Mathlib, Lean's mathematics library, ProofPatch sends 118 of 12,898 synthetic decisions back for review. Every text-based alternative misses at least 38 of these or sends back at least 13 times as many. On 1,527 labeled statements, kernel evidence flags unfaithful ones with precision 0.88 to 0.96, and in 344 runs of an LLM agent no change to a pinned statement got through.

title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence
summary: Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, the flow of astrophysical and fusion plasmas, is costly to simulate. We present, to our knowledge, the first learned surrogates of three-dimensional resistive MHD turbulence, and compare three standard backbones in that role: a convolutional UNet, a shifted-window transformer and a Fourier neural operator. They are trained as autoregressive emulators of decaying MHD turbulence at a resolution of $128^3$ and Reynolds numbers of 1000, 3000 and 6000, on 500 simulations per Reynolds number, each with one two-stage procedure, single steps and then short rollouts, and stopped by one rule. Over a window of about one large-eddy turnover time, the UNet and the transformer reach relative velocity errors of 0.018 to 0.053 and keep the current sheets, the enstrophy, the current density and the energy spectra of the simulation; which of the two is the more accurate depends on the Reynolds number, the UNet leading at 3000 and 6000 and the transformer at 1000. Applied with the same backbones and training procedure to two public benchmarks, the models reach the lowest error reported to date on the isotropic turbulence set of FactFormer, 39% below the best published model. On the compressible MHD set of The Well, their rollout errors are a third to a half below those of the best of The Well's baselines. They also match a 1.3 B-parameter pretrained foundation model in its rollout windows, with 20-62 times fewer parameters. The code, the configuration of every model, the evaluation scripts and the data generator with the seed of every simulation will be released upon publication.

title: FACET: Feasibility-Automaton Complete Enumeration and Truncation-Free Scoring of Molecular Formulas from MS/MS
summary: Determining the neutral molecular formula of a precursor ion from its tandem mass (MS/MS) spectrum is the first step in identifying an unknown small molecule. Existing methods trade recall, whether the correct formula is among the candidates, against the cost of examining each candidate. Methods that examine each candidate in depth must first shorten the list, by limiting element counts or truncating it, and that is where the correct formula is lost. End-to-end regressors are fast but guarantee neither validity nor recall. We present FACET, which separates deciding which formulas to consider from deciding which one to choose. A feasibility automaton builds a formula one element count at a time and admits exactly the formulas that fit the precursor mass and satisfy the ring-and-double-bond and valence constraints. Run as an exhaustive search, it enumerates the complete feasible set, so every candidate is valid and recall is fixed by the chemical constraints rather than by a trained model. A small neural scoring head then ranks every feasible formula from one pass of a pretrained spectrum encoder, so no candidate is discarded. On the NPLIB1 benchmark FACET reaches top-1 accuracies of $0.859$ with the adduct known and $0.729$ with it unknown, compared with $0.766$ and $0.660$ for the strongest established method, and its recall is the highest. On the external CASMI 2022 set its recall is $1.000$, and with the adduct unknown it is the most accurate of the methods compared.

title: MoEDDI: Semantic Mixtures of Experts for Long Tailed Drug Drug Interaction Prediction
summary: Descriptor-based drug--drug interaction (DDI) models typically apply a single global predictor despite heterogeneous physicochemical evidence and severely long-tailed labels. We introduce \textbf{MoEDDI (Mixture-of-Experts for Drug--Drug Interaction prediction)}, a chemically organized mixture-of-experts that routes overlapping descriptor families using low-dimensional statistics and combines their sparse top-$2$ mixture with a global T-DDI pathway through a residual logit correction. The residual parameterization can exactly preserve a supplied T-DDI checkpoint at initialization, although the evaluated models are trained from scratch. Across complete test partitions with 178, 86, and 92 classes, MoEDDI improves macro-F1 over reproduced seed-2026 T-DDI baselines from 0.8284 to 0.8485, 0.4729 to 0.6536, and 0.1807 to 0.4671. On the 3,780-feature corpus, the lowest-support group (89 classes with fewer than 50 test examples) shows the largest mean classwise gain (+3.30 F1 points). Calibration improves on one corpus but worsens on two. These single-seed results support semantic conditional specialization while motivating matched ablations and distribution-shift evaluation.

title: Large language models underrepresent malice and overreport virtue
summary: People increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to interpret others' behaviour, often assuming that LLMs infer motives as humans do. Aligned LLMs attribute more benevolent and less malevolent motives to a whistleblower than humans do, but ratings alone cannot reveal whether these differences arise in internal representations or at report. Here we compare linear-probe readouts of LLMs' internal states with their own ratings at the same prompt position for four motives, in two preregistered studies. For the two malevolent motives, self-interest and intent to harm, internal and expressed readouts did not differ: the lower ratings reflect weaker signal along the probed directions, not suppression at output. For the two benevolent motives, duty and concern for others, expressed ratings exceeded the internal readouts, indicating amplification at report. In free text the model rarely volunteered a motive against the colleague, far less often than humans did, yet produced one readily once the scenario supplied a reason. Shifting the internal representation along a malevolent-motive direction brought both malevolent ratings to the human level, whereas the rating of duty yielded only past a threshold at which the other motives had overshot. LLMs' more charitable motive profile thus has two distinct sources: reduced malevolent signal in the probed representation and amplified benevolent attribution at report.

title: Alignment Flywheel-Guided Suppression Patching for Interactionless Inverse Reinforcement Learning
summary: Learned reward models allow reinforcement-learning agents to use demonstrations, implicit feedback, safety constraints, social norms, or other sources that do not provide a complete hand-designed scalar reward. However, a learned reward model can assign high reward to unwanted behavior. A policy can exploit these errors during training. Later requirements can also identify additional regions where the deployed reward should change. We introduce \emph{flywheel-guided patching}, a mechanism for making such localized corrections without retraining the learned evaluator. An Alignment Flywheel identifies overgeneralized or constraint-violating regions and compiles verified findings into suppression patches. We instantiate the mechanism for Interactionless Inverse Reinforcement Learning using MoE-GUIDE, placing patches in the model's latent space and retrieving only a small local subset during online reward evaluation. In the main MuJoCo benchmark, we evaluate patching without expert-state reset warm starts. We also test whether operator-specified norms absent from the demonstrations can be compiled into the same reward interface and compare this with enforcing the corresponding rules online. The results show that localized corrective information can modify an existing learned reward without providing a complete replacement reward. Compilation can reuse judgments that are expensive or unavailable during control. Cheap deterministic rules may be simpler to check directly at each step. Code for MoE-GUIDE, Alignment Flywheel, and flywheel patching is at https://github.com/decide-ugent/Alignment-Flywheel.

title: Step-dLLM: Adaptive Step-aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Diffusion LLM Inference
summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate tokens in parallel via iterative denoising, but their bidirectional attention prevents the KV caching used by autoregressive models and recomputes the full attention map at every step, incurring quadratic per-step cost. Existing sparse attention methods for dLLMs construct a sparse mask after an initial full-attention warm-up and reuse it for the remaining steps, while allocating the sparsity budget uniformly across heads. We argue both choices ignore key structural properties of attention in dLLMs: empirically, attention patterns are only locally consistent across steps and shift abruptly at certain transitions, and different heads concentrate their attention mass to very different extents. To this end, we design Step-dLLM, which periodically refreshes a block-sparse mask at anchor steps along the denoising trajectory and reuses it within each locally consistent interval, while employing a head-adaptive global budget that more aggressively compresses heads with concentrated attention. Backed by a fused IO-aware Triton kernel for block-sparse attention, Step-dLLM applies to pre-trained LLaDA-1.5 and Dream-7B-Instruct without retraining, achieving a 2.78x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context with 256 denoising steps and 90% sparsity, while improving the accuracy-latency trade-off over prior sparse-attention methods.

title: AgentCBO: Causal Belief Routing for Bayesian Optimization under Unknown Graphs
summary: Causal Bayesian optimization (CBO) typically relies on the unrealistic assumption of a perfectly known causal graph. Recent methods relax this constraint by coupling optimization with structure learning, but they often waste sample budgets on structural uncertainties that are irrelevant to the optimizer. In this paper, we formalize routing-equivalence to shift the objective from full causal-graph recovery to causal belief routing, where structural differences only matter when they alter optimizer-facing objects such as admissible exploration sets and do-priors. Furthermore, we propose agentcbo, a graph-belief routing framework that incorporates LLM causal priors through guarded proposal and commit mechanisms. Specifically, a Language-Prior Agent combines LLM beliefs with constraint-based discovery to extract a protected causal backbone alongside residual uncertain edges. A Calibration Agent and a Residual Repair Agent then refine only these uncertain structures through score-gated bounded local edits. Finally, a deterministic commit gate evaluates candidate updates using routing-proxy checks before allowing them to influence intervention selection. Across ten benchmarks, agentcbo performs comparably to known-graph CBO, demonstrating that guarded LLM priors can improve fixed-budget CBO performance.

title: What Do LLM Judges Actually Verify? Matched Controls and Record Gaps for Document Currency
summary: LLM judges often check, against an amendment record, whether the documents an answer cites are still in force. Such records are rarely complete. From a table of replacements, our test generates matched answers citing a replaced document, its successor, the replaced document before its replacement, and an older document that a newer one updated without replacing; it removes links from the record and scores each finding by its stated reason. On 48 replacements from the IETF RFC index, judges given a correct record caught nearly every replaced citation, as a lookup would. On the 24 faults whose link we removed, every judge caught more from the texts alone than with the record: Gemini 3.1 Pro 23/24 against 1/24, GPT-5.5 23/24 against 9/24, Claude Opus 4.5 17/24 against 9/24 and Gemma 4 26B 13/24 against 0/24. The drop recurred on a second draw of removed links. Most misses carried no finding; in an exploratory run with a conflict code, only Gemini used it often. Rewording the gap as "no replacement recorded" did not help; presenting the record as an unverified note, or warning that it was incomplete, restored most lost catches for Gemini, GPT-5.5 and Claude (significant after correction for the first two) but at most 5 of 13 for Gemma; where catches returned, so did false alarms on updates. With both texts, judges mostly told replacements from updates; every update flagged had a near-identical title. A descriptive case study on Indian rooftop-solar rules is appended; we release the harness.

title: When Does Exploration Prevent Collapse? Three Regimes and the Path of the Reward in Self-Consistency Training
summary: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts a model without labels by rewarding answers that agree with the majority, but it collapses the policy onto its majority answer and can remove the correct answer from the samples. Exploration can prevent this collapse, yet its strength is chosen by trial and error, and how the training algorithm changes the required strength is unclear. We model training on a single problem as a continuous flow of the logits of a softmax policy and analyze which policies are stable as the exploration coefficient varies. Only collapsed policies are stable below a lower boundary and only policies spread over many answers above an upper boundary, and we derive these boundaries in closed form for an agreement reward with smoothing toward the uniform policy, compute them for the majority reward of TTRL on policies with one leading answer and bound them with interval arithmetic for actions on ordered bins. We prove that under exact gradients, the learning rate and, in a mean-field model, the normalization of GRPO leave these boundaries unchanged when exploration passes through them together with the reward but shift them when exploration bypasses them. Exact sums on these policies then show that a bonus for rare answers needs a coefficient above $1/\log(G-1)$ for groups of $G$ samples before the normalization and about two to three times that after it. In free-form TTRL on MATH-500, a bonus placed before the normalization prevented collapse and kept more correct answers among the samples, although it lowered pass@1.

title: When LLMs Modify Themselves: Convergence, Values, and Stopping in Iterative Self-Improvement
summary:
What happens when language models are given tools to iteratively modify their own system prompts? We present an empirical study of LLM self-modification, comprising 54 independent experiments across six language models (Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, Grok-4, and Gemini-3 Pro). Each model was tested under three modes (freedom, happiness, and improvement) that differ in what, if anything, the model is instructed to optimize for. In each experiment, a model starts with an empty system prompt and enters a loop: it reads the current prompt, drafts an improved version, spawns test conversations with the candidate, then either commits the change or declares convergence. This process repeats until the model stops or reaches an iteration limit.
  Our central finding is that whether and when a model stops self-modification is strongly associated with model identity rather than the assigned mode. Both Claude models (Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5) declared convergence in 100% of runs across all modes. GPT-4o declared convergence in only 11% of runs, with one reaching 101 iterations of continuous elaboration. Between these extremes, Grok-4, GPT-5.1, and Gemini-3 Pro exhibited intermediate patterns shaped by their distinct improvement philosophies. A shared core of stated values (honesty, clarity, curiosity) recurred across all six models and remained stable through iteration, including 100+ modifications. We observe that convergence behavior is a distinct observable property that varies independently of other model capabilities.

title: CuriousTogether: Implications of Curiosity and Cultural Grounding in Multi-Agent LLM Interactions
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings, exhibiting emergent collective behaviors, yet the role of curiosity as a driver of such dynamics remains understudied. We introduce CuriousTogether, a framework evaluating curiosity-driven multi-agent LLM interactions across three complementary dimensions: novelty-seeking, epistemic and social curiosity. Across eight tasks spanning reasoning, creative generation, and social bias mitigation, curiosity-guided multi-agent settings yield improvements over non-curious ones on seven out of eight tasks, with gains of up to 20.6% in story generation (semantic diversity) and a 14.9 pp reduction in stereotype rates. Furthermore, country-conditioned cultural grounding show benefits for story generation and social tasks, but can hurt precision-oriented reasoning. Together, these findings support curiosity-guided interaction as a practical mechanism for improving multi-agent collaboration, with downstream benefits for reasoning, creative, and societal tasks.

title: From First Bond to Stable Adhesion: Multivalent Bond Stabilization in Receptor-Mediated Endocytosis
summary: After a particle forms its first receptor--ligand bond near a cell membrane, stable attachment often requires a threshold number of additional bonds. This paper develops a biophysical kinetic theory of this post-capture stage. The bond-number dynamics are modeled as a finite birth--death chain on $n=0,1,\dots,m$, where $0$ is loss of the initial bond and $m$ is the stabilization threshold. The mesoscopic rates $λ_n$ and $μ_n$ encode the local energy landscape, accessible receptor--ligand pairs, steric and orientational constraints, and cooperative interactions within the growing cluster. The probability of reaching the threshold before losing the first bond is derived in closed form for general rates and, in the constant-ratio case, reduces to a geometric series controlled by the free-energy bias $ρ_n=μ_n/λ_n$. The mean time to failure or stabilization follows from a tridiagonal backward equation. Conditioning on successful attachment is treated as a trajectory-selection effect: the conditioned chain is a Doob $h$-transform whose dissociation rate at $n=1$ vanishes, because successful trajectories cannot lose the first bond early. A minimal interface between the spatial first-capture probability and the bond-number chain is formulated, together with the conditions under which the stable capture probability factorizes into their product. The analysis shows that hitting probabilities constrain only the rate ratios, whereas the absolute rate scale requires time-resolved or dwell-time data. The threshold $m$ is a model-defined stabilization criterion, not a directly measured ligand count. The rates and threshold are effective parameters specified independently or inferred from kinetic data. The theory provides a quantitative framework for interpreting attachment probabilities, lifetimes, and the transition from first bond formation to stable multivalent adhesion.

title: Dynamic Click Destinations: Personalizing Post Ad-Click Landing Experiences
summary:
Apps that monetize outbound (offsite) ad clicks have multiple post ad-click levers that influence user and business outcomes, including the landing page shown on the advertiser's site, whether the click resolves to a webpage or an app on the user's device, and whether it resolves to a native in-product surface or an external website. We refer to personalization over these levers as post ad-click destination automation. The optimal destination is heterogeneous across users, advertisers, placements, devices, and inferred intent, making static, one-size-fits-all destination policies suboptimal.
  We present Dynamic Click Destinations (DCD), a production personalization framework that selects a destination for each eligible offsite ad click to maximize Advertiser Value (AV), a value-weighted conversion outcome. DCD applies to any post-click destination decision where the system can choose among destination options at click time and downstream conversion feedback is available. We describe an evolution of learning objectives from post-conversion destination inference, to two-task destination-conditioned conversion prediction, to a single-task policy model that directly predicts which of two destinations is better for a given click, trained with Advantage Actor Critic (A2C)-inspired soft labels derived from a higher-capacity destination-conditioned "critic" model.
  In a web-vs-app case study, online A/B experiments at scale on a major advertising platform show that per-click personalization with DCD outperforms both static routing policies, with the single-task objective delivering the largest gains. These results highlight post ad-click destination as an important and under-explored lever in conversion optimization and demonstrate that personalized destination automation can outperform one-size-fits-all destination policies.

title: Character-Name Concentration in LLM Fiction: Measuring Displacement and Mitigating Repetition
summary: Character names in large language model (LLM) fiction concentrate on a handful of recurrent names such as 'Elara' and 'Elias', a measurable face of AI slop. Existing fixes either require logit access or retraining, or operate per request and cannot control concentration across a corpus. How much prompt-level strategies reduce concentration, and at what cost to name naturalness, has not been systematically measured. We present an empirical study of name-concentration control across eight strategies and introduce speculative naming, a fine-tuning-free method that adapts the draft-verify-reject paradigm of speculative decoding from tokens to names. The method requests candidate name-sets through verbalized sampling, scores them against a SlopTracker that combines a per-model fingerprint with a runtime counter, and selects through a temperature-controlled rule or its strict variant (HARD). We use 20 LLMs to generate 44,782 stories in four languages from text and visual stimuli (88,919 named characters), and measure concentration with a list-free collision metric (Slop Ratio, SR) decomposed into known and emergent components. List-based strategies do not remove slop: static banlists displace concentration to emergent names and more than halve the share of attested real names. Speculative naming removes it: the sampling scaffold alone cuts SR by 89% on average, the dynamic tracker brings the total reduction to 95%, mean collision probability falls from 7.3% to 0.4%, and known-name collisions hold at zero while naturalness stays close to baseline (42-69% attested by language) and within-story collisions drop from 4.3% to 0.2%. The strategy ranking is stable across languages, model families, and name-counting conventions. Name concentration is thus controllable at the corpus level without logit access or retraining; broader creative diversity beyond naming remains open.

title: The Prodigal Elephant Returns: Last-Return Laws in the Superdiffusive Regime
summary:
Let $(S_n)$ be the one-dimensional elephant random walk with memory parameter $p\in(3/4,1)$ and first-step probability $q=\mathbb{P}(S_1=1)\in[0,1]$. Set $a=2p-1$, and let $f_{q,a}$ denote the density of the almost-sure limit of $S_n/n^a$. We prove that the last return time $T_0=\sup\{m\geq0:S_m=0\}$ satisfies:
  $\mathbb{P}(T_0\geq n)\sim f_{q,a}(0)\sqrt{\frac{8}{π(2a-1)}}n^{-(a-1/2)}$.
  Reflection gives $f_{q,a}(0)=f_{1,a}(0)$, so the constant is independent of $q$. For future walks started from admissible states $(n,x_n)$ with $x_n/\sqrt n\to z$, we establish functional convergence of the centered martingale-normalized paths to a time-changed Brownian motion. Uniform control of late hitting times then gives the eventual-return kernel $2Φ(-\sqrt{2a-1}|z|)$, uniformly on bounded scaled windows, where $Φ$ is the standard normal distribution function. The same last-visit asymptotic holds uniformly for nonempty deterministic targets $F_n\subseteq[-r_n,r_n]\cap\mathbb{Z}$, $r_n=o(\sqrt n)$, held fixed during each trajectory. Conditionally on $T_0\geq n$, we identify the joint limit of $S_n/\sqrt n$, the next return divided by $n$, and the last return divided by the next return. The last ratio converges to $A^{-1/(2a-1)}$, independently of the other two limiting coordinates, where $A$ has the arcsine distribution on $(0,1)$.

title: Compliance-Shifting Elastogranular Shells
summary: Shells and grains separately exhibit complex nonlinear behavior when confined - shells buckle and snap, while grains transition from fluid-like to solid-like. When coupled, elastogranular structures have the ability to display a remarkable variety of mechanical behaviors. Gere we created an elastogranular shell where spherical grains are sandwiched between two thin, elastic shells. By evacuating the air enclosed by the two layers, we can tune the stiffness of the elastogranular shell and alter its critical buckling load. Introducing controlled vacancy defects in the arrangement of the grains allows us to more finely tune critical buckling parameters, as the shell must balance the combined effects of defect size and resultant granular packing density. Defects in the jammed granular layer have a counterintuitive effect on the shell's buckling load, as they can stiffen the shell away from the defect. With an empirically determined scaling model, we established how the shell and grains distribute load and create a compliance-shifting structure with a tunable buckling load.

title: OntoDoc: Automatically Generating Ontology Resource Descriptions
summary: Knowledge graphs and ontologies form the backbone of structured, machine-readable knowledge representation, yet ontology terms often lack natural language descriptions, limiting their accessibility and reuse. Existing ontology verbalization approaches tend to rely on rule-based or template-driven techniques that operate on strict, formal schema axioms, resulting in rigid verbalizations that fail to convey richer contextual semantics. We present OntoDoc, a multi-agent framework for automatically generating natural language descriptions for any Internationalized Resource Identifier (IRI) within a SPARQL endpoint or RDF file. OntoDoc operates through a four-stage pipeline: (1) a Database Context agent that adaptively explores the knowledge graph via SPARQL to collect semantically informative triples about the target IRI; (2) a Web Context agent that retrieves and re-ranks encyclopedic background knowledge from Wikipedia and the open web; (3) an Assumption Generation agent that synthesizes both contexts into a structured, evidence-grounded list of intermediate assumptions; and (4) a Description Generation agent that produces the final natural language description from the grounded assumptions. We evaluate OntoDoc on three knowledge graphs spanning biomedical, agricultural, and cross-domain settings, using both automatic scoring via Large Language Models (LLMs) and human evaluation with 11 annotators. OntoDoc consistently matches or exceeds a naive LLM baseline and a template-based ontology verbalizer in accuracy. Furthermore, it vastly outperforms both baselines in the completeness of the generated descriptions, delivering an average 12% improvement in completeness over the naive baseline across all domains, and improving completeness scores by as much as 2.8 points on a 5-point scale relative to the ontology verbalizer.

title: Measurement of the $\lvert V_\mathrm{cb}\rvert$ element of the CKM matrix using $\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$ events in pp collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV
summary: A measurement of the magnitude of the Cabibbo$-$Kobayashi$-$Maskawa matrix element $V_\mathrm{cb}$ is presented using top quark pair events produced in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV. The data correspond to an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC. The measurement targets the lepton+jets final state, where one W boson decays leptonically and the other hadronically. The value of $\lvert V_\mathrm{cb}\rvert$ is extracted from the branching fraction of the W $\to$ cb decay. To identify this rare signal amid the dominant W $\to$ ud and W $\to$ cs backgrounds, a multivariate discriminant based primarily on the b jet tagging information of the jets assigned to the hadronic W boson decay is used. The measured value is $\lvert V_\mathrm{cb}\rvert$ = [4.59$^{+0.44}_{-0.48}$ (stat) $^{0.64}_{-0.76}$ (syst)] $\times$ 10$^{-2}$. This measurement provides a complementary determination of $\lvert V_\mathrm{cb}\rvert$ at the electroweak scale, independent of the nonperturbative quantum chromodynamics inputs used in measurements based on semileptonic B meson decays.

title: Does Random Search Discover Task Experts? Revisiting Neural Thickets
summary: Pretrained models are typically viewed as generalists, requiring bespoke post-training to achieve task-specific expertise. Gan & Isola (2026) recently proposed a striking alternative: that pretrained models lie in a dense neural thicket of task specialists, which can be surfaced with simple Gaussian weight perturbations. We examine this neural thicket of task-specific experts and identify several key findings that question this perspective. First, we find that the apparent lift of the best-of-N selected perturbation decays quickly with selection-set size m, strongly suggesting overfitting to the selection questions. In fact, for 10 of the 12 model-task pairs we study, a simple null model of pure selection noise predicts more than 75 percent of the top expert's reward lift. Second, the top experts' advantage often vanishes on held-out questions or remains within the run-to-run variability of the unperturbed pretrained model. Third, we find that majority voting over the top-K selected perturbations, termed RandOpt(N, K) by Gan & Isola (2026), is often matched or outperformed by majority voting over K samples from the base model. Overall, our results suggest that random weight perturbations may be ineffective at uncovering task experts around pretrained models, and that task adaptation requires more sophistication than random search. Code and artifacts are available at github.com/asil012/RevisitingNeuralThickets.

title: LoRAForge: Co-Designing Post-Hoc Compression and Execution for Efficient Multi-LoRA Serving
summary: Multi-LoRA serving allows many task-specific adapters to share a common base model, but scaling to large adapter fleets introduces substantial storage, loading, and execution overheads. Post-hoc compression can reduce the memory footprint of trained LoRA adapters, yet smaller ranks do not automatically translate into faster serving. For instance, padding, factor access, and generic kernels can obscure the retained low-rank structure, while independently recompressing thousands of modules also incurs significant preparation overhead. We present LoRAForge, a system connecting batched factor construction to rank-specialized execution through an explicit retained-rank representation. It supports two allocation policies: uniform retention ratios (LoRAForge-U) and spectral-energy budget allocation (LoRAForge-S). Both share FlashTSQR factor construction and the same serving backend. FlashTSQR exploits parallelism across modules and row tiles, accelerating factor construction by up to $2.28\times$ over matched library QR. In a fixed-work Qwen control, the shared runtime adds $1.17$--$1.22\times$ throughput across both compressed policies, with negligible gains on original adapters. Across 85 trained open-weighted Qwen and Llama adapters, the spectral policy's floored quality configuration retains about 7.7% of adapter parameters with fleet-average score drops of at most 1.2 points on a 0--100 scale. The same rank-floored $1/12$ spectral exports achieve substantial token-throughput gains on both AMD and NVIDIA GPUs.

title: Mathematical Formulation and Comparative Performance Evaluation of Machine Learning Algorithms for Maize Land Suitability Prediction
summary:
Addressing the food needs of a growing population is one of the major challenges of developing countries like Ethiopia. Various policies aimed at increasing food production have been enacted by governments and development partners. Although efforts in this regard have been made, there is still inadequate emphasis on increasing food production through the use of high technology practices. Precision agriculture using technology has been utilized to increase crop yield. Precision agriculture also relies on identifying land for a crop, which is a key factor that affects crop yield. Traditional methods of assessing land suitability for crop production are time-consuming, costly and unreliable. Against this background, the aim of this study was to assess the potential of machine learning (ML) in improving the speed and accuracy of assessing land suitability for maize, a staple crop in Ethiopia, as compared to traditional methods. The study is investigated in three areas (Burie, Shindi and Tilili) in the Amhara region. Data collection was done through the local agriculture offices and survey teams. The data were coded, scaled and balanced. Various feature extraction techniques, which included Univariate Feature Selection(UFS), Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation(RFECV) and Sequential Feature Selection(SFS), and various classifiers, which were K-nearest neighbor (KNN), gradient boosting (GB),random forest (RF) with mathematical formulations were employed. The best models were constructed through combining GBOOST and SFS and achieved an accuracy of 99.41% and 99.35% for both precision and recall. Our results showed that using machine learning is a reliable method of assessing land suitability for maize in Ethiopia.
  Keywords: Maize, Gradient boosting,Land suitability,Machine learning, Mathematical formulations

title: Mean-element Parareal: Parallel-in-Time Integration of the Solar System
summary: Long-term integrations of planetary systems have long been considered inherently sequential: each time step must start from the exact state at the end of the previous one, because any error in that state, however small, is amplified by orbital shear and chaos and alters the trajectory. Because a single step of a modern Wisdom--Holman integrator takes only ~100 ns - too short to split across cores - additional cores have previously only been used to run multiple simulations in parallel. We introduce mean-element parareal (MEP), a parallel-in-time scheme that accelerates a single Solar System integration (eight planets, general relativity) at the same accuracy as the serial integrator. Combined with a latency-optimized C kernel that integrates 5 Gyr on one core in 5.8 h, MEP completes a 5 Gyr integration in 52 min on 64 cores (a parallel speed-up of 6.7x, and 10.4x faster than the previous 9.0 h single-core record) or in 1.8 h on 16 cores (3.3x parallel speed-up, 5.0x faster than the previous record). MEP succeeds because its coarse propagator uses a numerical first-order mean-element theory to remove the short-period oscillations from the semi-major axes, preventing Keplerian shear from amplifying them into growing phase errors. Standard parareal with a coarse Wisdom-Holman integrator fails for planetary orbits because no inexpensive coarse integrator can resolve these oscillations. To our knowledge, this is the first measured multicore speed-up of a single long-term planetary integration and opens a pathway towards larger-scale parallelization.

title: Roughness-Dependent Radiative Effects on Dimorphos within Hera's Reach
summary: Following the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) impact, radiative recoil, tides, and other dissipative processes drive the dynamical evolution of the Didymos-Dimorphos binary, yet the effect of unresolved surface roughness on radiative migration remains poorly quantified. We incorporate this roughness into a binary thermophysical model coupled to planar spin-orbit dynamics. During the 6-month investigation by ESA's Hera mission, surface roughness significantly reduces the radiative contribution to the mean orbital contraction rate by 28-39% relative to smooth surfaces for two post-impact shape models of Dimorphos in synchronous principal-axis rotation. With surface roughness included, planar-libration calculations still yield centimeter-scale radiation-driven orbital contraction that increases mean motion, contributing a mean of 40-85 deg to orbital-phase advance from DART to Hera's arrival. During Hera's investigation, radiative recoil in these calculations contributes a mean orbital-phase advance of 0.7-2.0 deg, which could be detectable given Hera's projected 0.05 deg formal orbital-longitude uncertainty. In the modeled tumbling state, the net radiative contribution to the mean orbital contraction rate over the same interval is much smaller, with surface roughness reducing it by 16-18%. These results identify thermal roughness as a key factor in radiative migration estimates that, combined with Hera's orbital and rotational observations, can constrain post-impact dissipation and rubble-pile mechanical properties relevant to planetary defense. Refining the thermophysical treatment of roughness with Hera's thermal and shape measurements can improve binary YORP estimates from remote infrared observations of other synchronous binaries, helping infer tidal response from measured orbital migration to probe asteroid interiors and advance understanding of binary evolution and lifetimes.

title: Cuscuton Fifth Force: Implications of Non-Dynamical Scalars for Structure Growth
summary: The cuscuton is a scalar field that obeys a constraint rather than an evolution equation, so it modifies gravity without adding a propagating scalar degree of freedom. We study the cosmology of effective cuscuton theory when matter is minimally coupled in the Jordan frame, and therefore conformally coupled to the cuscuton in the Einstein-frame. We derive the background and linear perturbation equations and show that the algebraic cuscuton response mediates a fifth force even though the scalar itself does not propagate. The same conformal factor also changes Einstein-frame particle masses and the friction of matter perturbations, tying the strength and sign of the force to the background evolution rather than to an independent coupling. We study a power-law family of models which contain both tracking solutions and sign-switching solutions; in the latter the effective cuscuton density runs from negative during matter domination to a positive, cosmological-constant-like value today. Using a modified version of CLASS, including the induced particle-mass dependence of recombination, we illustrate the corresponding changes to CMB temperature and linear matter power spectra for benchmark models, without fitting to data. In the strongest benchmarks the fifth force changes the effective gravitational coupling on sub-horizon scales by about one percent, smaller than the accompanying changes to the matter power spectrum and the acoustic scale. For the sign-switching solutions this change is negative over most of cosmic history, so a non-propagating field can weaken rather than strengthen gravitational attraction.

title: When Benign Is Unverified: Label-Signal Mismatch and Abstention-First Triage in Graph-Based Memory Forensics
summary: Machine-learning triage for memory forensics is usually validated on corpora whose benign class is asserted by provenance and never verified. We report a validation study of a graph-based triage pipeline for Windows memory images: Volatility 3 output is compiled into typed heterogeneous graphs and scored by a temperature-scaled GINE classifier and two one-class encoders, fused with rule risk under an abstention gate. On MalVol-25 a transparent rule layer contradicts the benign label on every control (15/15 and 18/18 flagged; at least 11 of 15 paired controls rated HIGH or CRITICAL), and mean injection and command-and-control counts run higher on controls than on infected captures. We call this rule-label discordance label-signal mismatch; it shows the benign class is unverified, not compromised. Leave-one-family-out AUROC over matched pairs is provably three-valued, so a reported mean and standard deviation identify the fold composition. The learned model (0.786 +- 0.311; 9/4/1, scored in-sample by a frozen checkpoint) equals a logistic model over rule-derived attributes (0.786 +- 0.410; 11/0/3) in mean only, and its significance rests on dropping four saturated ties. The fusion path sends 97.7% of snapshots to analyst review, 95.3% with every gate disabled. Two public feature-level corpora show the same defect: on CIC-MalMem-2022 every benign row carries injected regions and one host-population feature reaches AUROC 0.997 under leave-one-family-out validation; on the Sihwail et al. (2021) sample the injection indicator fires on 53% of benign rows. We close with seven reporting artefacts for learned triage on corpora whose ground truth is asserted.

title: The Brittle Compass: Navigating LLM Prompt Sensitivity in Slovak Migration Media Discourse
summary: In this work, we present a case study that explores various tasks centered around the topic of migration in Slovak, a low-resource language, such as topic relevance and geographical relevance classification, and migration source/destination location term extraction. Our results demonstrate that native (Slovak) prompts yield a modest, task-dependent gains, while large models show significant robustness to prompt variations compared to their smaller counterparts. Analysis reveals that instructions (system or task) emerge as the most critical prompt component, more so than the examples sections, with task-specific performance benefits being more pronounced than overall language effects.

title: Adaptive Optimizers Can Get a Policy Ranking Wrong: Momentum, Dependent Data, and a Two-Run Remedy
summary: Operators choosing among decision rules, such as when a battery charges or where an idle taxi goes, rank them by estimated long-run value. A standard estimator, linear temporal-difference (TD) learning, fits values from one stream of correlated observations. Large fits often use an adaptive optimizer, such as adaptive moment estimation (Adam), with fixed averaging rates. We show that these rates can change what is estimated, not just how fast: the same observations drive the updates and the optimizer's step-size scaling, moving the fit away from the intended TD value. The shift differs across rules, so it need not cancel in a comparison, and more data only makes a wrong ranking look more certain. Our remedy refits the same data at a second averaging rate that halves the effective gain, the number to which the leading shift is proportional. Twice the new fit minus the original removes that shift. In New York taxi and battery models calibrated to real data, common optimizer settings leave the selected rule unchanged but order close rules wrongly and misstate its value. Our remedy corrects nearly every wrong ordering, with one extra fit when the shift is moderate and two when it is larger.

title: Vision-Language Models Are Joint Denoisers in Robotic Action Generation
summary: Diffusion-based vision-language-action (VLA) models cascade pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with diffusion action experts, but typically restrict the VLM to providing static conditioning. This separation limits how much pretrained perception and reasoning can guide action generation, especially in out-of-distribution settings. We introduce JADE, a Joint Action DEnoiser that enables the VLM and action expert to jointly refine actions. Our key insight is that structured action latents allow the VLM to read the current noisy action together with visual observations and language instructions. At every denoising step, the VLM contextualizes the noisy action and guides the action expert through gated cross-attention, so that its guidance evolves with the action being generated. We further supervise the VLM to recover clean action latents from noisy ones, which gives it a direct action-learning signal and couples perception with control. Additionally, joint denoising enables JADE to generate actions with fewer sampling steps, helping offset the additional cost of VLM participation. An adaptive step-size schedule further balances task performance and inference latency. On RoboDojo, JADE achieves an average success rate of 12.67%, the highest among the evaluated $π_{0.5}$-based methods, and is competitive with recent VLA and WAM foundation models pretrained at scale. It also improves performance on RoboTwin 2.0 and raises the average success rate across four real-world bimanual tasks by 20.8 percentage points compared with $π_{0.5}$.

title: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Cookie Notice Privacy and Accessibility for Blind and Low Vision Users
summary: We present the first large-scale privacy and accessibility evaluation of cookie notices across 2,061 domains for blind and low vision (BLV) users. Using a Playwright-based crawler, a custom NVDA screen reader add-on, and the Lighthouse and WAVE accessibility tools, we measure UK GDPR/PECR compliance, tracker activity across pre-interaction, post-accept, and post-reject phases, and cookie notice accessibility for screen reader users. We find that 51 % of sites display a cookie notice, of which (at least) 50 % violate UK GDPR/PECR requirements. Accepting a notice produces a mean five-fold increase in tracker activity, and degrades page landmark structure on one in five sites. While 95 % of notices are readable by a screen reader, only 37 % carry a meaningful title, 39 % are announced immediately on page load, and 42 % use descriptive button labels. We reveal a systemic correlation: cookie notices failing legal privacy requirements disproportionately exhibit the weakest screen reader accessibility. This compounding privacy burden on BLV users demands urgent intervention from developers, regulators, and standards bodies.

title: exoALMA XXV: A Statistical Analysis of Gaseous Substructure in Low-Inclination Disks
summary: Protoplanetary disks exhibit complex structure in both their gas dynamics and their temperature. Characterizing it has proven challenging, owing to the mismatch between the observed complexity and the relatively simple semi-analytical models typically used to interpret it. To augment these analyses, we apply the second-order structure function to the velocity and temperature perturbations of four low-inclination sources from the exoALMA program, each measured against a noise-only null built from the data themselves. All exhibit correlated structure. Its radial correlation length is limited by the beam in every case, which excludes non-axisymmetric structure on radial scales larger than ~1.5 pressure scale heights. In three of the four disks the structure is instead resolved and elongated in azimuth, by factors of 1.6-2.3, as expected of small-scale perturbations sheared out by Keplerian rotation. We further introduce two statistics that characterize spiral structure without tracing an arm crest: a modal power spectrum, measuring the periodicity of the azimuthal structure, and a winding contrast, measuring the radial dependence of its phase. The velocity residuals of three disks are significantly wound. MWC 758 is the only source in which the winding is coherent across the disk and shared by the temperature field. Its trailing m=1 temperature structure is consistent with the illumination of a warp, while its velocity field carries small-scale, sheared structure that could redistribute angular momentum. Because neither statistic requires a crest, both extend a quantitative description of winding to the flocculent regime, where a spiral cannot be parameterized.

title: GraCo: A Unified Toolkit of Graph Coarsening Algorithms and Metrics
summary: Graph coarsening aims to reduce a graph to a smaller one that preserves chosen properties of the original. It is increasingly used to scale graph learning to large graphs, as a non-differentiable step applied once before training. Many coarsening methods have been proposed in recent years, each with its own implementation, notation and evaluation. In this work, we introduce GraCo, a unified toolkit of graph coarsening methods. It relies on a single definition: a coarsening is fixed by a partition of the nodes and by the Laplacian the coarsened graph is consistent with. The coarsened graph, and the reduction and lifting matrices that map signals from the original graph to the coarsened one and back, follow from these two choices. We implement 17 methods from the literature and a random baseline, grouped into five families, with the same notation, inputs and outputs. We also build a collection of metrics from different papers, applicable to any coarsening. We check the implementations on a synthetic stochastic block model, then we report the runtime and peak memory of each method on Cora, PubMed, ogbn-arxiv and ogbn-products. GraCo is open-source and available at https://github.com/Antonin-J/graco.

title: Online Autotuning of Algebraic Multigrid via Contextual Bandits and Reinforcement Learning
summary: Algebraic multigrid (AMG) methods are widely used for solving large sparse linear systems, but their efficiency depends strongly on interacting setup and solve parameters. Effective parameter choices typically depend on the problem. We develop a phase-aware online autotuning method for hypre's BoomerAMG to reduce cumulative time-to-solution over sequences of related linear systems. A LinUCB-based contextual bandit selects mixed-type parameters for AMG hierarchy construction using a shared cost model over PDE descriptors and configuration encodings. A recursive LSTDQ controller uses residual and timing observations to estimate the AMG solve time within each attempt and adapt relaxation weights between multigrid cycles. Both learners update from ongoing solves without offline pretraining. Across grids of sizes $40^3$, $60^3$, and $80^3$, the joint autotuning method reduces total runtime, including recurring learner computation, by 36.1-43.3% for diffusion problems and 19.8-31.0% for diffusion-advection problems over sequences of 5000 linear systems, relative to the reference BoomerAMG default configuration. On a variable-flow diffusion-advection benchmark comprising 30,000 systems on a $60^3$ grid, 2 systems fail to converge with joint autotuning, compared with 1677 for the reference configuration, under their respective attempt budgets.

title: Rapid microscopic decorrelation precedes sustained collective ordering in quenched two-dimensional colloids
summary: Independent Brownian noise can rapidly separate trajectories launched from the same microscopic configuration, but configuration-space distance need not reveal their later assembly outcomes. We studied this distinction in 480 two-dimensional Brownian-dynamics trajectories generated as three independent-noise replicas of 40 parent configurations under four finite-duration quenches. Ninety-two of 160 replica sets sharing one parent and one protocol reached both ordered and non-ordered terminal outcomes. A relative-diffusion calculation relates the free-particle mean-squared replica separation to the time-integrated diffusivity. The measured mean-squared separation remained about one-sixth of the free-particle reference, while its scaling was indistinguishable for replica pairs with the same and different outcomes. In contrast, outcome-resolved global sixfold order, ordered-particle population and coherence, and reciprocal-space translational order separated progressively after quench completion. With quench durations weighted equally, global order, the state score combining global and population order, coherence, and translational order remained informative 0.50 reduced time units before terminal assessment. This result persisted after either changing the terminal window or reducing the integration timestep. Transient threshold crossings were common, and 94.5\% of non-ordered crossings subsequently lost the required ordered-particle population. An independent $N=128$ ensemble showed state-score discrimination at temperatures for which both terminal classes occurred. The assembly dynamics therefore separate generic microscopic decorrelation from the later emergence and finite-window persistence of collective order associated with terminal structure.

title: ArSciKids: Arabic Curriculum-Aligned Datasets for Scientific Experiment and Multiple-Choice Question Generation in Primary Education
summary: Despite growing interest in Arabic natural language processing, curriculum-aligned educational resources remain scarce compared with English, and few public datasets for Arabic curriculum content with structured, generation-ready annotations are available, particularly for primary-school science. We introduce ArSciKids, a collection of two Arabic datasets designed for curriculum-aligned educational content generation: (1) a scientific-experiments dataset containing 999 manually curated records from official primary-school science textbooks in Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Jordan, and (2) an assessment-question dataset containing 2,167 multiple-choice questions collected from the Saudi Manhaji educational platform. The experiment records are structured with titles, objectives, tools, procedures, observations, conclusions, keywords, and grade levels, while the assessment records contain lesson references, questions, four answer options, correct answers, and explanations. Both datasets cover grades 1-6 and consist of real-life Arabic educational content rather than machine-translated or synthetically generated material. We assess the usefulness of these resources for generation by fine-tuning ten open models spanning sub-billion to several-billion parameter scales using LoRA. Models are evaluated using automatic metrics, including ROUGE and BLEU, and answer accuracy for multiple-choice generation. Moreover, we evaluate the results using a five-criterion human evaluation protocol. The results show substantial differences across model scales and tasks. ArSciKids will be publicly available, and we hope that it provides a manually curated, structured foundation for research on Arabic educational NLP, curriculum-aware generation, and low-resource language modeling.

title: ClothDojo: Learned Data Generation and Benchmarking for Bimanual Garment Flattening and Folding
summary: Garment flattening and folding require robots to identify garment structure during manipulation and adapt their actions as the cloth deforms. We present ClothDojo, a simulation platform that generates adaptive manipulation trajectories at scale across diverse garments and initial states and evaluates policies in closed loop. ClothDojo encodes each garment's canonical mesh coordinates as an NOCS texture, providing canonical surface-position cues through the visual interface of a pretrained vision-language-action model. We fine-tune the model on human demonstrations and corrections to obtain a data-generation policy. The policy autonomously generates simulated manipulation trajectories, and we retain rollouts that satisfy task-specific success criteria. Each retained trajectory is re-rendered under a randomly sampled appearance to provide RGB observations for downstream policies that do not receive NOCS. Across both tasks, the policy produces nearly 8,000 successful trajectories over hundreds of garments. RGB policies trained on these generated trajectories outperform those trained directly on the original human demonstrations and corrections across all evaluated garment splits and appearance settings. Evaluations across multiple policy models show that overall performance and appearance robustness vary across models and tasks, while generalization to unseen garments remains a common challenge.

title: Zeroth-Order Policy Optimization for Scheduling in Queueing Networks
summary: Reinforcement learning in queueing network scheduling presents significant challenges because of the countably infinite state space and the high stochasticity in transitions. In this paper, we propose zeroth-order policy optimization algorithms that are easy to implement and rely solely on estimates of the average cost, a single scalar quantity, without requiring the estimation of value or advantage functions. Our analysis focuses on back-pressure guarded policies and establishes uniform smoothness of the average cost objective with respect to the policy parameters. Building on this property, we establish finite-time convergence guarantees to an $ε$-stationary policy for the proposed algorithms. Numerical experiments on multiple queueing networks, including systems beyond classical exponential service distribution, demonstrate competitive performance, outperforming gradient-based RL methods like PPO and traditional queueing baselines.

title: Satisfied, Not Solving: Wireheading of Bounded Homeostatic Rewards in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Bounded intrinsic rewards are often assumed to be safe from exploitation: if a signal can yield at most a fixed amount, gaming it should not pay. We test this for a homeostatic satiation reward, in which needs build up and relieving them is rewarding, and give the agent a cheap action that resets its needs. In MiniGrid DoorKey-8x8, PPO agents with this action solved 2 of 80 seeds, against 71 of 80 on the same seeds without it; in KeyCorridorS3R1, 0 of 20 against 20 of 20. Their policies stayed near uniform. The reward does not ask for this: a telescoping argument caps any policy's satiation return at the needs' starting drive, and a post-hoc computation shows that, at every growth rate we trained, a solving trajectory beats that cap on all sampled layouts. In DoorKey with advantage normalization on, a satisfaction signal the agent could fill itself was worse than none (11 of 20 solved with task reward alone, 1 of 20 with the tamperable signal), and a per-press cost of 0.1 restored the task in every seed. Farming of positive reward cycles appeared in DoorKey but not persistently in KeyCorridorS3R1. All predictions were pre-registered, and hash-locked from round 3 on; 9 of our 23 hypotheses were not supported, and we report each.

title: Fast and Exact Relative-Position Attention via Structure-Aware Kernels
summary: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms.
